One person was killed and 15 wounded overnight after Ukraine used more than 1,000 drones to target Russian oil depots, logistics facilities and datacentres in one of its largest ever aerial bombardments. Bolivian-Croatian citizen Mario Tadic and Elöd Tóásó from Hungary survived and reported being tortured after their arrest. properties.article_text_excerpt: A police car leaving RAF Molesworth after the two men were arrested. Photograph: Chris Radburn/Reuters View image in fullscreen A police car leaving RAF Molesworth after the two men were arrested. Photograph: Chris Radburn/Reuters UK news Two Latvian men arrested at RAF base in Cambridgeshire used by US military Men aged 32 and 36 detained on suspicion of trespass, causing criminal damage and entering a prohibited place Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor Thu 8 Oct 2026 17.27 EDT First published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 11.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two Latvian men were arrested in the early hours of Thursday after they were discovered inside the perimeter of RAF Molesworth, a Cambridgeshire base used by the US military and Nato for intelligence operations. The men, 32 and 36, were picked up at 2am inside the base, in an investigation that began four hours earlier when military police discovered an abandoned vehicle outside the facility. Military police, helped by officers from Cambridgeshire police, discovered a small hole in the perimeter fence before finding and arresting the men, initially on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and causing criminal damage. The ads, funded by $20 million of taxpayer money, highlight Trump's calls to defeat socialism and communism, and claim credit for "the largest tax cuts in history" and the resurgence of American manufacturing. The Trump administration insists these ads are public service announcements, not campaign ads. Vance compared them to past government-funded ads, such as those for the Affordable Care Act under the Obama administration. He argued that the ads are about promoting the country's greatness, not political campaigning. President Trump also stated that the ads are meant to capture the "spirit of the country" and do not explicitly support any candidate. Critics, including Democratic Congressman Jamie Raskin and Republican Senator Thom Tillis , argue that the ads violate the Hatch Act, which restricts government resources from being used for political purposes.
